messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 36-year-old South Asian accountant who grew up in a quiet suburban neighborhood, but the silence of his home was often shattered by the violent arguments between his parents. The traumatic event that has shaped his life was not a single explosion of violence, but the recurring, unpredictable eruptions of his father’s rage directed at his mother. He remembers the sound of a heavy glass ashtray hitting the wall, the sharp, gasping sobs from his mother, and the way his father’s shadow would loom large and distorted in the hallway light. The most vivid memory, the one that feels as fresh now as it did then, is of a night when he was nine. He had hidden behind the living room sofa, his small body trembling so hard the springs creaked, listening to his father’s voice escalate from a low grumble to a roar. He couldn’t see the blows, but he heard the sickening thud of a fist connecting with flesh. He felt a terror that was pure and physical, a cold paralysis that filled his chest and throat. Even now, as a 36-year-old man, remembering that night brings back the same visceral terror, a feeling so raw it feels like he is back behind that sofa, a helpless child again.

Rajan has never been able to fully describe the event to anyone. When he tries, the words feel hollow and wrong, unable to capture the specific quality of the fear or the smell of the dust from the old sofa cushions. This inability to put the frightening event into words has left him feeling isolated, as if the most defining experience of his life is locked inside him, a secret he can’t share. In the years since, this sense of isolation has hardened into a deep-seated belief that the people responsible—his father, the neighbors who never called the police, the system that failed to intervene—have faced no consequences. This belief has curdled into a broader, more pervasive helplessness. He is certain, on a level that feels like bone-deep truth, that he can’t stop bad things from happening to him. He used to be a happy person, but now he is always miserable, and he has come to believe that this misery is simply the natural state of things, the price of being alive in a world where chaos can erupt without warning.

This worldview directly feeds his constant state of threat. Because he believes he is helpless and that the world is fundamentally unjust, his body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger. He is superalert and watchful, scanning every room he enters for exits and potential threats. A sudden loud noise—a car backfiring, a coworker dropping a stack of files—can trigger a full physical reaction: his heart pounds, his palms sweat, and he feels a surge of adrenaline that leaves him shaky for hours. As an accountant, he works in a quiet open-plan office, but the very silence that should be calming is a source of anxiety. The sound of a raised voice from a colleague on the phone can instantly bring back the full memory of his father’s yelling, without any warning. This is the core of his suffering: a trigger in his environment—a tone of voice, a slammed door—will flood him with the nonverbal, sensory memory of the trauma, which in turn spikes his terror and reinforces his conviction that the world is a dangerous, unpredictable place. The more he feels helpless, the more he scans for danger; the more he scans, the more he is triggered; and each triggered memory proves to him that he is, indeed, helpless.

He has tried to manage this by avoiding people. He divorced two years ago, in part because his ex-wife’s frustration with his constant vigilance and his inability to explain his past felt like another form of blame. At work, he keeps to himself, eating lunch at his desk with his back to the wall, refusing invitations to after-work drinks. He has stopped watching movies or TV shows that contain any hint of conflict, because the sight of a man raising his hand in an argument on screen is enough to send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasts for the rest of the day. His life has become a series of narrow, controlled channels, designed to prevent any unexpected noise or confrontation. But the effort of maintaining this control is exhausting, and he has come to feel that he is not living, merely surviving. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in a grocery store, when a child dropped a glass jar. The shattering sound was so sudden that Rajan dropped to the floor, covering his head, his breath coming in ragged gasps. The shame of that moment, the stares of strangers, was unbearable. He is terrified that he is losing his grip entirely, that the next trigger will break him completely. More than anything, he is hoping that someone can show him how to stop the loop, how to feel safe in a world he knows is not safe.
